ig_caption:
Your rating graph isn't broken. Ratings move in waves, even when your chess is steady.

Every game moves the number, and how much depends on who you played. Streaks turn up by chance, just as a coin can land heads five times running. Rating systems also swing harder when they are less sure of you: after a break, or early on. So judge your progress over months, not days, and only worry when a slide keeps going for weeks.

slides.title: Every game moves it
slides.body: Win and you gain points, lose and you drop. How many depends on your opponent: beat someone stronger and you gain more, lose to someone weaker and you drop more.
slides.note: So even a perfectly steady player's line zigzags, game by game.

slides.title: Streaks happen by chance
slides.body: Flip a coin twenty times and you will often see four heads in a row. Wins and losses cluster the same way, even when your skill hasn't changed.
slides.note: A bad week is not proof you've got worse.

slides.title: New ratings move faster
slides.body: Chess.com and Lichess use Glicko-style ratings, which track how sure they are about you. Early on, or after a long break, each game swings the number more.
slides.note: Back after a month off? Expect bigger jumps both ways.

slides.title: Zoom out
slides.body: One day's line says little. Compare your rating now with three months ago, or a year ago. That is where improvement shows.
slides.note: Many climbs look like staircases: a jump, a flat stretch, another jump.

slides.title: What a real slump looks like
slides.body: A small dip is normal noise. A slide that keeps going for weeks is worth a look: are you tired, rushing, or trying a new opening?
slides.note: Review a few recent losses before you change anything.

slides.title: Every wave is on the poster.
slides.sub: Your whole rating history, on one print.
